nodes.title: Digital Services Act study on financial scams on online platforms and ways to counter them
nodes.tldr: Digital Services Act study on financial scams on online platforms and ways to counter them Anonymous (not verified) Tue, 10/20/2026 - 08:47 A new study maps the main types of onlin...
nodes.details: Digital Services Act study on financial scams on online platforms and ways to counter them Anonymous (not verified) Tue, 10/20/2026 - 08:47 A new study maps the main types of online financial scams, platform features scammers exploit, their impact on users and society and measures platforms can take to stop them. Online financial scams – fraudulent schemes whose primary aim is to extract money from victims – have grown into a pervasive crime in the digital age. They are present across all types of online intermediary services, including Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Search Engines (VLOSEs). The European Commission has procured this study in 2025 to support its supervisory and enforcement tasks under the Digital Services Act (DSA). It provides a typological mapping of financial scam formats across online platforms and assesses existing and emerging mitigation strategies to curb financial scams online. The study was carried out by Open Evidence and Spark Legal and Policy Consulting. It does not evaluate compliance by providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs. Read the study and the executive summary in (French and English). Key insights A diverse typology of scams The study maps different types of online financial scams and categorises them in six broad categories: investment scams romance scams e-commerce scams employment and collaboration scams unexpected gain scams disaster relief scams The study finds that investment scams and romance scams are the most common and fastest-growing forms of scams in Europe. It also finds that the scam landscape is increasingly being redefined by overlapping methods across different categories. Online platforms features and financial scams The study presents information on relevant features related to scams on online platforms including: advertising systems recommender systems content moderation of organic content monetisation systems app store content and private messaging functions inauthentic identities and account manipulation deceptive commercial content generative AI The study also shows how financial scams operate across different platforms and are facilitated by organised criminal networks that sell tools and services, effectively lowering the barrier to entry. Identifying effective countermeasures The study identifies relevant countermeasures across 4 categories: Access and gatekeeping measures, such as know your business customer and identity requirements are the first line of defence against online financial scams; Detection and removal measures, including automated and human-review based measures, can neutralise scam content; User facing measures – such as reporting tools and information on redress – can equip end users with tools and information to identify and report online scams; Platform-level policies and cooperation with third parties can help platforms identify, prevent and address online scams. Related topics Online platforms and e-commerce DSA - Digital Services Act

nodes.title: First harmonised standard supporting the AI Act published in the Official Journal
nodes.tldr: First harmonised standard supporting the AI Act published in the Official Journal Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 10/19/2026 - 09:37 The European Commission has published the referen...
nodes.details: First harmonised standard supporting the AI Act published in the Official Journal Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 10/19/2026 - 09:37 The European Commission has published the reference to the first harmonised standard supporting the implementation of the AI Act in the Official Journal of the European Union. The standard, EN 18286:2026 - Artificial intelligence - Quality management system for EU AI Act regulatory purposes, developed by CEN and CENELEC, provides a clear legal pathway for providers of high-risk AI systems to comply with the quality management system requirements under article 17 of the AI Act. Its publication through Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274 means that providers implementing this standard will benefit from a presumption of conformity with the Article 17 requirements covered by the standard. EN 18286 translates these requirements into an operational quality management system (QMS). It is the only AI QMS standard with a presumption of conformity. It is mapped to Article 17 of the AI Act, built around the AI system lifecycle – rather than the organisation – and designed to be layered on top of the existing international standards – such as ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 9001 or a sectoral QMS (e.g. ISO 13485) – rather than replace them.  EN 18286 explicitly allows providers in regulated sectors to integrate management systems, rather than run separate ones. Organisations without ISO/IEC 42001 that plan to place or put into service high-risk AI systems in the EU market can use EN 18286 to expand an existing QMS or build one that fulfills the requirements of article 17 requirements. The publication of this standard marks an important milestone in implementing the AI Act, ahead of the application of requirements for high-risk AI systems, with further harmonised standards expected to follow. Find further information about the Standardisation of the AI Act. Related topics Artificial intelligence

nodes.title: Commission holds special meeting of Scientific panel on frontier AI safety and risks
nodes.tldr: Commission holds special meeting of Scientific panel on frontier AI safety and risks Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 10/09/2026 - 09:16 The Commission holds a special meeting of the ...
nodes.details: Commission holds special meeting of Scientific panel on frontier AI safety and risks Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 10/09/2026 - 09:16 The Commission holds a special meeting of the Scientific Panel on artificial intelligence (AI). The panel has been investigating recent loss-of-control incidents, and together with the Commission’s AI Office, has worked on a set of questions for the companies that developed the models involved. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, will attend the meeting. The Scientific Panel brings together 60 world-leading independent experts who advise the EU AI Office and national authorities on systemic risks, model classification, evaluation methodologies, and cross-border market surveillance. During the meeting, the panel will present recommendations to the Commission on frontier AI safety and security risks. Executive-Vice President Henna Virkkunen said: “The EU has the first law in the world that addresses systemic risk from AI, and we need state-of-the-art scientific input. AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, but with a strong legal framework, decisive enforcement and the best scientific minds supporting this work, Europe can lead in ensuring safe and secure AI.” Find out more about the Scientific Panel on artificial intelligence (AI) Related topics Artificial intelligence AI Act scientific panel Related content News article12 October 2026Special meeting of the AI Scientific PanelOn 9 October 2026, Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, and Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh, Chair of the AI Scientific Panel, convened a special meeting.
